{"id": "5d4cfd40-1ff2-45b1-9e20-5807161444b8", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Confirmed the standard rate: **NAT Gateway data processing is $0.045/GB** (plus the separate hourly charge, which doesn't change based on volume).

Here's the math on the traffic you've identified:

| | |
|---|---|
| Traffic going to your own VPCs via NAT | ~12,000 GB/month |
| NAT data processing rate | $0.045/GB |
| **Monthly savings on NAT processing** | **~$540/month (~$6,480/year)** |

A couple of things worth flagging as you plan the fix:

- **This is the NAT-processing savings only.** If that 12,000 GB is also incurring regular EC2/VPC data transfer charges (cross-AZ or inter-region), those charges are separate from NAT and apply either way — moving off NAT doesn't eliminate them.
- **The replacement path matters for net savings.** Routing inter-VPC traffic via VPC peering is the cheapest fix — same-AZ peered traffic is free, cross-AZ peered traffic is billed at the standard ~$0.01/GB data transfer rate (not $0.045), so you'd still net real savings. Routing through a Transit Gateway instead adds its own data processing charge (~$0.02/GB) plus attachment hourly fees, which eats into the savings — worth comparing before you pick an approach.
- **The $0.045/hr NAT Gateway hourly charge stays** unless you remove NAT gateways entirely, which isn't likely since you probably still need it for actual internet-bound traffic.

So a reasonable floor estimate is **~$540/month** in NAT processing savings, with the realized number depending on whether the replacement path (peering vs. Transit Gateway) adds any new data transfer cost. Want me to look at your actual VPC topology to see which of your VPCs are peering candidates vs. would need a Transit Gateway?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
